description.summary: The pan-European nightmare spirit — the 'mare' from which English 'nightmare' (literally 'night-mare') is derived. A malicious entity, typically female, in Germanic and Slavic folklore that 'rides' people's chests at night.
description.full: The Mare is the broad pan-European nightmare spirit known in Germanic, Scandinavian, and Slavic folklore. The English word 'nightmare' itself preserves the term: nyght-mare in Middle English meant a 'mara' visiting at night. The mare is described as a malicious entity, typically female, who sits, walks, or 'rides' on the chest of a sleeping person, causing bad dreams, suffocating sensations, sweating, and the experience now identified as sleep paralysis. The word descends from Old English mære and Old Norse mara, both from Proto-Germanic *marōn, ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning 'to crush' or 'to press'. The same element entered French as -mar in cauchemar (caucher 'to press' + mare). In Scandinavia, the earliest narrative reference is in Snorri Sturluson's Ynglinga saga (c. 1230), which describes the death of King Vanlandi by a mara conjured by the Sámi sorceress Huld. In German tradition the mare is closely linked to the Alp (Albtraum, 'alp-dream', is the standard German word for nightmare); in Polish and Czech tradition, the zmora / můra may be either a demonic being or the involuntarily wandering soul of a living person. Modern sleep medicine identifies the underlying experience as sleep paralysis with hypnagogic hallucination.

etymology.origin: Old English mære, Old Norse mara, Old High German mara, all from Proto-Germanic *marōn, ultimately from a PIE root meaning 'to crush, press, oppress'.
etymology.meaning: 'Crusher' / 'oppressor' — the spirit that presses on the sleeper's chest.
etymology.first_use: Attested in Old English and Old Norse from the early medieval period; the compound 'nightmare' is attested in Middle English from the late 13th–14th century.

related_phenomena.name: Mara
related_phenomena.description: Continental and Slavic spelling of the same nightmare spirit

related_phenomena.name: Alp
related_phenomena.description: German nightmare creature; German Albtraum 'alp-dream' = nightmare

features.description: Typically appears as a young woman or an old hag
Can transform into animals (cat, dog, owl) or objects (straw, mouse) in Polish and Scandinavian tradition
'Rides' or sits on the sleeper's chest

physical.morphology: Insubstantial spirit, often invisible; when seen, appears as a small, often female figure entering through keyholes or chimneys.

abilities.description: Source of the experience that gave English 'nightmare' its name
Sits on the sleeper's chest, producing the sensations characteristic of sleep paralysis
In Scandinavian tradition the mare may 'ride' a victim through the night, leaving them exhausted by morning
Said to ride and tangle the manes of horses, giving rise to 'elf-locks' / 'witches' stirrups'

patterns: Visits sleepers at night, particularly when they sleep on their back
Repelled by iron, brooms placed crosswise, upside-down slippers, or food offerings
Sometimes blamed for tangled hair and matted horses' manes

range.description: Across Germanic-, Scandinavian-, and Slavic-speaking Europe, with cognates and continuations into modern French (cauchemar) and many other languages.

first_recorded.source: Old English and Old Norse usage

peak_activity_periods.description: Mare folklore widely attested across Germanic and Slavic Europe.
Mare folklore continues alongside Christian incubus / succubus framings; documented in detail in Polish and Czech sources.

origins.cultural_roots: Proto-Germanic and Proto-Slavic dream and night-spirit tradition organised around a 'crushing' spirit.
origins.earliest_accounts: Old English and Old Norse usage from the early medieval period; the Ynglinga saga (c. 1230) records the earliest narrative incident.
origins.folklore_connections: Closely connected to the German Alp, English Old Hag, Latin incubus / succubus, and to non-European sleep-paralysis traditions such as Japanese kanashibari and Newfoundland Old Hag tradition.

timeline.event: Snorri Sturluson's Ynglinga saga records King Vanlandi's death by mara
timeline.significance: Earliest narrative reference to a mare in Scandinavian literature
timeline.source: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga, ch. 13

timeline.significance: Modern English word 'nightmare' enters the language

timeline.event: Henry Fuseli paints The Nightmare, depicting an incubus on a sleeper's chest with a horse looking on — visual touchstone for the European mare tradition
timeline.significance: Defining image of the mare in Western art

history.modern_era: The mare survives chiefly as etymology — English 'nightmare', German Albtraum, French cauchemar, Polish zmora — and as a touchstone for cross-cultural sleep-paralysis research.

notable.name: Death of King Vanlandi (Ynglinga saga)

location.description: Uppsala, in the legendary tradition of the Yngling kings (recorded c. 1230)

credibility_factors: Recorded in a major medieval Scandinavian source

notable.description: Snorri's Ynglinga saga relates that King Vanlandi Sveigðisson of Uppsala was killed by a mara conjured by the Sámi sorceress Huld at the bidding of Vanlandi's abandoned wife Drífa. As Vanlandi slept, the mara 'trod on his legs'; when his men seized his head, the mara 'pressed down on his head' and crushed him to death.

factors: Recorded centuries after the events it purports to describe
credibility.notes: The earliest recorded mare narrative in Scandinavian literature.

sources: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga, ch. 13

documentary.name: Ynglinga saga in Heimskringla
documentary.description: Snorri Sturluson's account of the death of King Vanlandi at the hands of a mara is the earliest extant narrative record.
documentary.analysis: Read by historians as a literary preservation of pre-Christian Scandinavian sleep-spirit tradition.
documentary.source: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga, ch. 13

paranormal.name: Genuine sleep-spirit
paranormal.description: The mare is a real spiritual being who attacks sleepers, as understood in pre-Christian and folk-Christian Germanic and Slavic Europe.
proponents: Germanic, Slavic, and Scandinavian folk tradition
evidence_cited: Continuity of the experience across language families

scientific.name: Sleep paralysis with hypnagogic hallucination
scientific.description: The mare is a folkloric interpretation of the well-described physiological state of sleep paralysis, in which REM atonia persists into wakefulness and is accompanied by chest-pressure sensations and visual or tactile hallucinations.
evidence_cited: Strong correspondence between mare symptoms and clinical sleep paralysis

skeptical.name: Cultural elaboration of a physiological experience
skeptical.description: Mare folklore is a culturally specific elaboration of a universal physiological experience.
evidence_cited: Convergent symptoms across unrelated traditions (Old Hag, kanashibari, etc.)

traditions: Old Norse and Scandinavian mare tradition
Polish zmora and Czech můra traditions
stories: Polish tales of identifying a zmora by joined eyebrows
Folk practices of placing brooms or upside-down slippers by the bed
folklore.beliefs: Across Germanic and Slavic Europe the mare was treated as a real cause of bad dreams and chest-pressure, requiring protective measures.

literature: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Deutsche Mythologie (1835)
games: The mare appears as a recurring nightmare-spirit figure in fantasy games (Persona, The Witcher, Final Fantasy)
other: Etymological source of English 'nightmare' and many cognates across Europe
Henry Fuseli, The Nightmare (1781) — defining visual depiction

researchers.name: Jacob Grimm
researchers.contribution: Treated the Mare in detail in Deutsche Mythologie (1835), placing it within Germanic mythology

researchers.name: J. Allan Cheyne
researchers.contribution: Studies of sleep paralysis as the experiential basis of mare-type traditions

research.ongoing_studies: The Mare is studied within Germanic and Slavic philology, comparative folklore, and the cognitive science of sleep paralysis.

sources.title: Sleep paralysis and the structure of waking-nightmare hallucinations
